options: TypeScript only recognizes discriminated unions if the common property is named `kind` rather than `type`.
The discriminant property `type` was given the broad type `string` rather than a literal type like `"login"`, preventing TypeScript from identifying it as a discriminated union.
Interfaces cannot form discriminated unions; only type aliases declared with `type` can have discriminant properties.
The union members must be converted into runtime classes before narrowing can take effect.
objective: Construct discriminated unions with common literal discriminant properties

options: TypeScript silently compiles and skips the `default` case at runtime whenever a `PushNotification` is encountered.
TypeScript raises an error at the `switch` header because switch statements over unions cannot have a `default` case.
TypeScript converts `PushNotification` to `any` in the default branch, deferring any error until runtime.
TypeScript raises a compile error in the `default` branch because `notification` has narrowed to `PushNotification`, which is not assignable to `never`.
objective: Enforce compile-time exhaustive switch checking over discriminated unions using the never type in the default case

stem: Why does assigning the switch subject to a variable of type `never` in the default case guarantee exhaustive checking at compile time?
options: The `never` type instructs the TypeScript compiler to automatically generate code for unhandled variants during compilation.
Narrowing removes each handled variant until no possibilities remain, producing `never`; if any variant is unhandled, it retains that variant's type, which cannot be assigned to `never`.
All types in TypeScript can be assigned to `never`, allowing the compiler to perform a runtime assertion.
Assigning to `never` causes JavaScript to throw a runtime SyntaxError when an unhandled case is encountered.
objective: Enforce compile-time exhaustive switch checking over discriminated unions using the never type in the default case
